title: Draupadi's Cry as She Is Dragged and Disrobed
story:
One throw of the dice had cost Yudhishthira his kingdom, his brothers, and himself — and then, in the madness of the game, his wife.

It had happened at Hastinapura, in the hall of the Kurus, where Yudhishthira had been drawn into a game he could not win. He had staked his wealth and his kingdom; he had staked his brothers, one by one; he had staked himself. And when nothing was left to stake, he had staked Draupadi — and lost her too.

Now Duryodhana, flushed with winning, commanded the herald: 'Go, bring Draupadi here. You have nothing to fear from the sons of Pandu.'

The herald went unwillingly, like a dog entering a lion's den, and told the queen that she had been won in the game and must come to the house of Dhritarashtra to do menial work.

Draupadi looked at him. 'What prince is there,' she asked, 'who stakes his wife? The king was certainly mad with the game. Could he find nothing else to stake?'

'When he had nothing else,' said the herald, 'he staked you. First his brothers, then himself, then you.'

'Then go back to that gambler in the assembly and ask him one question,' said Draupadi. 'Whom did he lose first — himself, or me? Find that out, and then come and take me.'

The question was not a delay; it was the hinge of everything. If Yudhishthira had lost himself before he lost her, then he was no longer his own master — and a man who does not own himself cannot stake his wife. The whole right of the Kauravas' claim turned on the answer.

The herald carried the question to the hall, where Yudhishthira sat among the kings like a man robbed of his wits and gave no answer, good or ill.

'Let the princess of Panchala come here and put her question herself,' said Duryodhana. 'Let everyone in this assembly hear the words that pass between her and Yudhishthira.'

So the herald went back a second time, more distressed than before. And Draupadi answered with what she had always held: 'Morality is the one highest object in the world,' she said. 'If it is cherished, it will bless us. Let it not abandon the Kauravas. Tell them I will do whatever the elders, who are virtuous and conversant with what is right, tell me.'

The herald repeated her words in the assembly. And the kings and elders sat with their faces downward, and not one of them spoke — for they all knew the eagerness and the resolution of Dhritarashtra's son. Yudhishthira, bound by his own promise, sent word that she should go before her father-in-law and weep; but that was not a rescue, and everyone in the room knew it.

Duryodhana had no use for questions or for morality. 'Dussasana,' he said, 'this herald fears Bhima. Go yourself, and bring the daughter of Yajnasena here by force. Our enemies are in our power now. What can they do to you?'

So Dussasana rose, his eyes red as blood, and went into the dwelling of those great warriors. 'Come, come,' he told the princess, 'you have been won by us, and won rightly. Accept the Kurus for your lords, and come to the assembly.'

And when she would not come, he seized her and dragged her into the hall before the gathered kings — before her husbands, before the elders who had lowered their faces — and in the sight of all of them, he began to strip her.

And it was then that Draupadi cried out. Not to the assembly, which had chosen silence. Not to her husbands, who sat bound and helpless. But past all of them, to the one name that could cross the distance:

'O Govinda, who dwells in Dwaraka! O Krishna, who is fond of the cowherds of Vrindavan! O Kesava, do you not see how the Kauravas humiliate me? O Lord, husband of Lakshmi, lord of Vraja, destroyer of all afflictions, O Janardana — rescue me, who am sinking in the Kaurava ocean!'

The cry rose through the hall and out of it, past the walls of Hastinapura, toward a city by the sea. The assembly heard it; the sky heard it. Whether anyone in Dwaraka heard it, the hall could not know — but the cry had gone out, and some cries are not finished when they end.
reflection: Draupadi's question — whether Yudhishthira had lost himself before he lost her — is the one true test the assembly is offered, and the kings fail it in silence. Her cry that follows is not argument but address: she stops pleading with men and names the one who can cross the distance, and the naming itself is the whole of her faith.
next_story_tease: But the cry had not gone unheard — in Dwaraka, the one who heard it had already begun to move.
hero_scene: In the Kaurava assembly at Hastinapura, Dussasana drags Draupadi before the gathered kings and strips her, while Draupadi, one hand raised, cries out toward the sky with the name of Krishna on her lips and the elders sit with lowered faces.

Draupadi questioning the herald, calm and intent
